stories.body:
Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports

T he pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon.

“Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braised sábalo fish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong.

Each man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers.

The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money.

In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation. Mining equipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street.

“We developed this town,” Zhang says between gulps of beer and bites of pork. “Without the Chinese, there would be no Mayaya today.”

As record gold prices drive Amazonian deforestation and violent conflict, these small-scale, private mining operations are tightening China’s grip on the world’s gold reserves. The Guardian spent five days with Chinese miners, investors and traders.

The Bolivian Amazon has long attracted foreign capital, from rubber and timber industries to North American mining companies in the 1950s. But now, Chinese mining is defining a new era of extraction, as a global network of goods, machinery and labour often thrives illegally under Bolivian law.

A 2014 national law limits mining rights to cooperatives and independent miners, state-controlled firms and domestic and foreign private companies. Such foreign firms must have a registered Bolivian office and operate in their own name. The state permits joint ventures, leases and risk-sharing agreements between foreign and national firms, but only through public-private contracts, in which the state is a shareholder.

Chinese mining firms operating outside this framework act unlawfully. Under a 2016 law , cooperatives also risk expropriation if they contract, lease or share mining-concession risks with foreign firms.

C hinese goldminers first arrived in Mayaya in 2005, but it was in 2017 that a major wave of immigration took place, after China’s national development and reform commission banned domestic small-scale gold mining , citing environmental and national defence concerns. The crackdown sent many miners and investors searching for work globally, and spurred several companies to hire workers from mines closed back home to work at newly opened operations in Bolivia.

One of those firms is Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export, which has operated in Bolivia since at least 2011. Officially, the firm does not carry out mining operations, listing only print materials and manufacturing in a supplier directory.

Campaigners say these companies skirt the law, “hiding behind” cooperatives to operate in Bolivia’s mining industry. On paper, foreign investors sign service contracts with local cooperatives, provide capital and machinery. In reality, they control the mines end to end, selecting sites, hiring workers, providing machinery, exporting gold and taking 75% to 80% of profits, says Alfredo Zaconeta, a mining researcher at environmental thinktank Cedla .

Behind these contracts, Zaconeta adds, Chinese investors evade legal responsibilities as the state lacks the resources and political will to oversee the mining lobby. He says it rarely, if ever, enforces existing ownership and permit rules.

As a result, in Bolivia, an entire economy has emerged to serve this migration, from La Paz lawyers specialising in Chinese work visas to a local phone store that doubles as an informal bank for exchanging bolivianos and renminbi. In some regions, Chinese miners recruit friends and family, forming home town clusters dedicated to the local mining industry.

Along Mayaya’s main street, shops sell all things Chinese – from bottled tea and cigarettes to pork intestines. Yang Yanbin, a Chinese investor, says: “As long as you have money to invest, this country welcomes you. We stuff all the money straight into our pockets.”

Chang Yuequan, a lifelong miner who has mined gold along the China-Russia border since his teens, is another Chinese investor in Mayaya. In 2017, after verifying Mayaya’s gold quality, he ordered 120 shipping containers from China and began assembling machinery.

In 2025, he opened his newest mine next to the Kaka River, which he named “Passion Fruit” in Spanish, referencing the wild vines covering the hillside. On one of his periodic visits, Chang and a Chinese employee watched an excavator in a huge pit claw soil into a loader before Bolivian workers blasted it with high-pressure hoses.

Chang says the workers then mix the slurry with mercury, then burn it to produce the final product: large, lumpy gold nuggets. Turning to the mine’s Chinese manager, Chang points to the green half of the hill and says: “This whole mountain is ours. Excavate that too.”

Chang’s friend and colleague, He Zijian, who ships gold from Mayaya to La Paz during price surges, confirms the Chinese influence in the region. He says: “Everything – down to the tiniest screws – is imported from China.”

The trade can be highly lucrative. Much of the gold from Mayaya ends up in Dubai via illegal exports. According to He, Chinese middlemen bring the bullion to Bolivia’s capital, La Paz, before smuggling it to the Gulf state. There, he says, the metal is sold at Murshid Bazar, Dubai’s largest gold market.

Gold in Dubai is often shipped further to Switzerland , where it is laundered into legal supply chains and sold in western markets. In July, police arrested a Bolivian man set to depart to Dubai from Santa Cruz, Bolivia. His four suitcases allegedly contained 189.5kg (418lb) of high-purity gold worth roughly £18.5m.

While the man arrested may not have links to Chinese mining companies, authorities say his arrest highlights the vast quantities of gold illegally exported from the country.

Jaime Sanabria, director of Bolivia’s mining regulator, Ajam , estimates that while Bolivia produces about 100 tonnes of gold a year, only about 10% is sold legally, costing the Bolivian government and the country’s people billions in lost revenue.

A longside illegal exports, the gold-mining boom has brought poor labour conditions and rapid environmental degradation. According to two dredge-boat miners, Bolivian workers are routinely paid a quarter of what Chinese workers doing the same jobs earn.

“They’ve left nothing for us,” says lifelong Mayaya resident Victoriano Piloy. “The money doesn’t stay here – that’s why we’re poor.”

In surrounding Indigenous communities, mercury poisoning has become increasingly common. Already hit hard by the climate crisis , deforestation and wildfires, residents often struggle to make a living through agriculture and fishing.

Many ultimately turn to mining, compounding mercury pollution. With Chinese companies controlling the river, Bolivian artisanal miners increasingly enter Madidi national park, one of the world’s most biodiverse. There have been tensions. In August, residents of a rural village south of Mayaya seized and burned mining machinery allegedly owned by a Chinese company, denouncing their environmental harms. Nearby municipalities have also banned gold mining .

“The environmental impact is devastating because no one is inspecting or enforcing the rules,” says Sanabria, the mining regulator, adding that about 80% of mining in the country is illegal.

While the government conducts environmental audits every year, Zaconeta says Chinese investors commonly receive advance notice and clean up before inspections. The decentralised nature of gold mining in Bolivia, with 3,117 cooperatives nationwide, complicates state regulation.

“It’s just a good faith declaration; it can’t be verified. Everyone knows they are breaking the law,” Zaconeta says.

The Ministry of Mining and Metallurgy did not respond to requests for comment. Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export Co and the Regional Federation of Gold Mining Cooperatives of Bolivia were also approached for comments.

Despite the criticism directed at the mining industry, under the country’s new conservative president, Rodrigo Paz, the trend is toward even more permissive policies . In May, Paz signed an agreement with mining cooperatives that reduces barriers to mining in protected areas and Indigenous territories.

Yet, government incentives may not be enough to ensure foreign companies’ long-term presence in Bolivia’s mines. Chang Yuequan, one of Mayaya’s early Chinese investors, has spent his life chasing the world’s best gold from Russia to Tibet and North Korea, and finally into the Bolivian Amazon. Twelve years in, he knows Mayaya’s gold is depleting. He expects to move on to his next destination in five or six years – once his boats stop operating.

At least a dozen Paceña beers into one of the Chinese investors’ frequent dinners, one investor sums up their worldwide reach: “You’ll encounter Chinese people in every corner of the world.”

Then his friend jokes: “We are just powerful like that – we could conquer the world!”

stories.body:
On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr , will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists.

The trial follows a conviction on October 27, when Attalah was found guilty of managing an unlicensed news website. The Mada Masr team had repeatedly applied for a license, but their attempts went unacknowledged. The proceedings took place in a single hearing, which Mada Masr states included serious violations of her right to a fair trial. She was sentenced to the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (approximately 55,000 USD), forcibly removed from the courtroom, and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered Mada Masr's closure and the confiscation of all equipment belonging to the organization.

The current wave of repression has also targeted Matsada2sh , a fact-checking and open-source intelligence initiative. Its entire six-person newsroom was violently arrested , illegally detained, and interrogated under torture before being charged with terrorism-related offenses and spreading false news. The team remains in pretrial detention.

According to CPJ, at least 25 other journalists are currently incarcerated in Egypt.

Governments seeking to control the flow of information increasingly rely on a combination of legal harassment, financial pressure, criminal prosecution, and restrictions on the infrastructure that makes independent publishing possible. Egypt's media licensing regime is a particularly troubling example. Requiring news organizations to obtain government authorization to operate creates an obvious mechanism for restricting who gets to publish and whose voices are allowed to reach the public.

The charge of spreading false news is similarly dangerous. Governments around the world have increasingly invoked the language of misinformation to justify restrictions on speech, often without meaningful safeguards against political abuse, as we laid out in our recent submission to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Governments should never be the arbiters of which reporting is permissible, particularly when that reporting concerns their own conduct.

Why Mada Masr matters

Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has spent more than a decade doing the kind of journalism that authoritarian governments find most threatening: documenting abuses, amplifying marginalized voices, and reporting on issues that powerful institutions would prefer remain hidden.

Its reporting has given torture survivors and the families of political prisoners a platform. It has opened space for debate about reproductive rights. It has brought frontline reporting from Sudan and Gaza, and stood alongside refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns.

Emerging as a digital-first publication, in a media environment where traditional outlets were increasingly constrained, being purely digital allowed Mada Masr’s founders to build an independent publication outside the structures of legacy media.

At a time when only 43% of Egyptians had access to the internet , going fully digital meant taking a big risk, but it was one that has been rewarding: Despite being blocked by the Egyptian government since 2017, Mada Masr has continued to reach Egyptian and global audiences, and Attalah has received numerous accolades, including the Knight International Journalism Award , the Ordre des Arts et des Lettres , and a spot in TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential people (2020).

Mada Masr has also consistently engaged with technology and advocated for a free and independent internet for the global majority. It has covered dozens of hot-button tech stories in recent years, from Egypt’s Cybercrime Bill and Israel’s use of AI weaponry in Gaza , to stories about the “ privacy chaos ” caused by biometrics to more personal essays about the importance of the internet and tech. In August, they launched an open call for proposals on original critical reporting on artificial intelligence.

Mada Masr may be thoroughly Egyptian, but it doesn’t belong just to Egypt. Its team has made into a publication that represents the kind of independent, local, grounded journalism that international audiences need, particularly at a time when international reporting on state repression is lacking. They built on-the-ground networks to center local voices in Sudan (publishing in both English and Arabic on the conflict) and Gaza out of a sense of cross-border responsibility and solidarity.

This is precisely why its potential closure should concern everyone who cares about a free press. The ability to publish independently, investigate powerful institutions, and to share information without government interference is fundamental to the exercise of free expression.

From solidarity to action

The international community has repeatedly expressed concern about restrictions on press and internet freedom in Egypt. More than 100 organizations have now joined statements of solidarity with Mada Masr, and with Matsada2sh .

These expressions of support matter, particularly when journalists are increasingly isolated and under threat—but solidarity must also translate into sustained political and institutional pressure.

The international governments and institutions that maintain relationships with Egypt—including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—should make clear that the prosecution of journalists and the forced closure of independent media outlets are unacceptable.

The cases against Lina Attalah, Mada Masr, and Matsada2sh must be dropped. The journalists who remain in detention must be released. And Egypt's licensing regime, with its profound chilling effects on access to information and independent knowledge production, must be brought to an end.

There is a particular urgency to defending independent media at a moment when governments are finding ever more ways to restrict the circulation of information. Whether through internet shutdowns, platform restrictions, surveillance, or the criminalization of reporting, the result is often the same: fewer opportunities for people to understand what is happening around them, to challenge official narratives, and to hold power accountable.

We cannot allow the closure of one of Egypt's most important independent newsrooms and the prosecution of its editor-in-chief to become another routine episode in the global erosion of press freedom. Nor should we wait until the last independent journalists have been silenced before recognizing what has been lost.

To learn more about Lina Attalah in her own reads, you can read our Speaking Freely interview from January 2026.

'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack

Published 2 November 2026, 11:21 GMT

Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.

Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".

He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.

Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.

"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.

The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.

In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.

Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.

In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.

The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.

Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.

Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".

An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food

In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.

A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".

"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.

One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."

The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.

Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.

The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.

The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.

In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.

A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.

A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

stories.title: Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
stories.summary: Dan Harrison was recorded as saying 76 council solicitors he branded "incompetent" would be made redundant.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Dan Harrison previously said his leaked remarks had been taken out of context

Published 2 November 2026, 16:07 GMT

The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.

Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.

He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.

It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.

In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.

Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.

The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.

In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.

"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.

"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."

Conservative group leader Deborah Taylor had called for an emergency vote to try to oust Harrison

Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.

He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.

Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.

Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.

"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."

He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.

"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."

Position 'untenable'

Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.

Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.

"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.

"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.

"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."

The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.

In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.

"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.

"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

stories.summary: A new action plan aims to rescue 2030 nature targets as financing remains inadequate.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A new action plan aims to rescue 2030 nature targets as financing remains inadequate.

The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.

Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.

The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.

The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”

“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

Catherine Weller, global policy director at the campaign group Fauna & Flora, said the Yerevan agreement was welcome but also noted that funding fell far short of a pledge that had been a key part of the 2022 deal. “In a world of trillionaires, we can certainly afford to spend $200 billion a year on protecting and restoring the very thing keeping us all alive: nature,” she said.

Conference organizers said governments, philanthropists, and businesses had announced close to $2 billion in new financial commitments to coincide with the Armenian gathering.

This included a commitment by the Netherlands to contribute $500 million to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazilian initiative to pay countries to keep their forests standing. The pledge was announced in the Dutch parliament the day after Brazilian leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected as president, to the relief of many attending the biodiversity summit.

After the close of the conference, Carina Pimenta, Brazil’s national secretary for bioeconomy, highlighted Lula’s record of protecting the Amazon rainforest and spoke of hope. “At a time of growing global uncertainty, the Yerevan Declaration sends a powerful message: world leaders recognise that protecting biodiversity is essential to food security, livelihoods, and economic resilience,” she said.

A growing number of countries to have drawn up national diversity plans, and the new pledge to the Brazilian fund, were “reasons for cautious optimism,” said Brian O’Donnell, director at Campaign for Nature.

But international funding for protected and conserved areas has fallen in a number of countries over years of disruption from war and high energy prices, with a 27 percent decline in environmental funding for the 2026-30 period.

stories.title: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
stories.summary: This DIY e-paper display works in two official ecosystems or on your own server.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
This DIY e-paper display works in two official ecosystems or on your own server.

One of the most useful gadgets in my kitchen is now a screen that never asks me for anything.

I recently bought a $48 DIY display kit from Seeed Studio (yes, that’s three E’s), developed in collaboration with TRMNL , that lets me display whatever I want, using whichever software ecosystem I prefer.

I previously built something similar by modding a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, which was selling for around $30 on eBay during a liquidation. The Lenovo device was only ever intended for business-to-business video, but it does a decent job of running a fork of LineageOS . Unfortunately, its limited RAM makes it sluggish. So when I came across the TRMNL kit and its e-paper display, I was sold.

I’d have an always-on display that shows me the information I want, with no subscription required. And since the screen populates automatically, I would never have to wrestle with a slow interface.

The Seeed Studio kit and TRMNL ecosystem aren’t trying to compete with products like the recently announced Apple HomeView , a $299 home hub designed to get the whole family interacting with it. If anything, the TRMNL kit is the HomeView’s antithesis. It’s designed to be entirely passive: The e-paper display stays on, cycling through potentially useful information on your desk or in your kitchen, from calendars and weather to news and all sorts of ideas thought up by its community members.

Here’s how it works.

Choosing a path

TRMNL, the platform company, was founded by indie hardware enthusiast Ryan Kulp in 2023 . Its first e-paper device launched via crowdfunding in 2024.

Seeed Studio provides the hardware. The established Shenzhen open hardware company is best known for its XIAO microcontroller boards.

In March 2025, Seeed teased an XIAO e-paper panel on social media, prompting a community member to ask whether it could run TRMNL firmware. The question brought the two teams together, and in July 2025, they announced an official partnership to develop a DIY e-paper kit combining Seeed’s hardware designs with TRMNL’s firmware packages.

Seeed designs and manufactures the hardware, while TRMNL maintains the firmware, plugins, and hosted service. But you’ll still need to make some decisions about how to set up the kit. There are three ways to get it running, depending on your budget and how comfortable you are with managing software yourself.

The stock TRMNL setup connects you with the company’s “ BYOD ecosystem ” (bring your own device), letting you use trmnl.com as your information server with a 14-day free trial. After that, you’ll need to pay a one-time $50 license fee to keep your device connected to TRMNL servers.

If you’d rather go your own way, Seeed offers software options, including Home Assistant compatibility, that don’t require a TRMNL connection or license. You can also access the SenseCraft Seeedash platform, which includes a plugin repository and design workspace. It’s worth checking out the options before committing to a $50 TRMNL license. The browser-based platform also includes a firmware-flashing tool Seeed describes as simple enough for anyone to use.

If you already have a server up and running, you can point the device right at it. Terminus is TRMNL’s open source container for this setup. The Terminus GitHub page describes the BYOS as providing “privacy first functionality by empowering you to run your own private server, network, and devices. You own the stack and the data.”

The e-paper display and control board simply ping an API to retrieve the information to display. You can even write plugins in HTML, which the screen renders as a bitmap. The trade-off is that your server needs to stay online, and maintaining it may bring some system-admin headaches some users may want to avoid. But hey, that’s why there are options.

What’s in the box?

XIAO ePaper Display Dev Board with XIAO ESP32-S3 Plus onboard

7.5-inch monochrome ePaper display (800 × 480 pixels)

FPC extension cable (10 cm)

FPC connector

2,000 mAh rechargeable Li-ion battery

Wi-Fi antenna

Two official case designs are available for 3D printing: a triangular prism and an L-shaped case. I went for the latter, and although I’d hoped assembly would be as simple as plugging everything in and slotting the pieces into place, it proved to be a bit more involved.

The kit came with all the hardware I needed, with one slight hiccup: I’d forgotten to order a case or display stand. Fortunately, TRMNL is a proper DIY project, and there are print files available for recommended stand setups. A quick print at my local library’s Bambu printer and $8 solved the problem. I probably should have chosen something other than “dealer’s choice” for the PLA color, as I ended up with a bright canary yellow device case. At least it stands out on my kitchen countertop.

I’d recommend trying the prism shell design over the L-style case I chose because the latter required me to cut a channel for the ribbon cable extension. It wasn’t a huge deal for a project like this, but you may need to do some extra work and fiddle with the fit. You’ll also need needle-nose pliers to remove the print’s support trees from the narrow space.

Assembly

Before trying to fit everything into the printed case, I wanted to make sure the hardware worked, so I connected the parts on my workbench. The case-less assembly couldn’t be simpler: Connect the battery or a USB-C power source, plug the display directly into the board, and you’re good to go. From there, connect your phone or tablet to the device’s Wi-Fi and enter your local Wi-Fi credentials.

If you attempt this build, be aware that it involves some delicate parts. The FPC is extremely fragile and can break if you force it to bend in a direction it doesn’t want to go (say, around the sharp angle of an L-shaped case). Getting the cable to conform to the design was challenging; I tried using tweezers to coax the cable around the bend but got nowhere fast.

Connecting and routing the ribbon cable extension was the most stressful part of the assembly. The case design just doesn’t accommodate the path the ribbon cable naturally wants to take. Following a helpful tip from a commenter on MakerWorld, I managed to snake the cable through the narrow passage by attaching a bit of paper tape to the end of the ribbon connector.

After powering on the kit for the first time, you’ll see the TRMNL logo and a QR code on the e-paper display. Scanning the code redirects you to a “ How to set up a new device ” guide written by Kulp, the TRMNL creator. The guide had been updated just 15 minutes before I clicked the link—a promising sign of a living document that is constantly evolving.

TRMNL.com

I wasn’t planning to use the trmnl.com service, but I wanted to get a sense of what it offered for its $50 access fee. The 14-day “free” trial is a misnomer, though. Before you can register your device, you’ll need to enter your credit card information and pay $1 for access. After plopping down a buck, the next screen welcomed me to my trial.

After registering your kit’s MAC address with trmnl.com, you’ll receive what the service calls a “friendly code,” a much shorter identifier that’s easier to remember than an entire MAC address. From there, you can install plugins to display content on a schedule throughout the day.

The options are vast. The marketplace contains standard fare like Google Calendar, weather, and stock quotes, alongside more niche offerings like rotating factoids about the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition in Star Trek .

If you’re looking for a hassle-free solution that “just works,” it’s hard to fault the package trmnl.com has put together. I’m a fan of any service that offers a one-time license fee over yet another forever subscription, and I think $50 is a fair price for the people behind the platform to be compensated for their work. After all, it handles all the rendering; the device simply displays information pulled from the APIs.

SenseCraft

On the Seeed side, there’s SenseCraft, a similar marketplace to trmnl.com’s but without the license fee. The website offers a browser-based flashing tool that promises to “flash official firmware from the browser. No coding. No terminal. Just clicks.”

The process was as simple as promised—once I figured out that I needed a USB-C to USB-C cable. I connected the board to my PC via the onboard USB-C port, opened the website in a Chromium-based browser (sorry, Firefox), selected my device from a drop-down menu, and clicked “Flash.” Once the device rebooted, setup followed essentially the same process as it did with TRMNL, minus the credit card. The tradeoff for free access is that Seeed is based in China and operates under its own privacy policy . Your call, but it’s certainly nice to have options.

After registering a Seeed account, I entered a code displayed on the device, just as I had with TRMNL. SenseCraft’s marketplace is similarly packed with community contributions, but I had trouble determining which plugins were intended for my device and which might not be compatible. I tried publishing several different feeds to the display, but I couldn’t get them to render.

SenseCraft leans heavily into AI-powered custom designs. While the platform offers a bit of everything, much of its content is geared toward the Chinese market, with English-language apps sprinkled throughout. I can see why US users reached out to ask about TRMNL compatibility.

Bring your own server

As TRMNL puts it, “the goal isn’t for BYOS to match parity with our hosted solution but to provide enough of a pleasant solution for your own customized experience.” Even a modest homelab server should have no trouble running the Terminus package, which acts as an API point that takes in information, renders the designs, and sends them to your e-paper display. The process shouldn’t put meaningful strain on most systems.

It’s great that there’s an “easy” version for a fee, but homelabbing is one of my favorite hobbies, and I love self-hosting projects wherever possible. When I first saw the DIY TRMNL/Seeed package, I was hoping I’d be able to control the feed myself.

For now, getting Terminus running on your server isn’t as simple as heading to your OS’s Docker app store and downloading a host service. TRMNL has a great guide to walk you through the setup, but if you’re not comfortable working with docker compose files, you may want to pay the one-time license fee and leave the hosting to TRMNL.

I won’t lie: I spent some late nights banging my head against the desk trying to get everything running. I’d initially tried hosting it on my main Unraid machine, but I kept running into bridge networking issues. The Terminus package is a multi-container compose stack with pieces like Sidekiq worker , Postgres , Valkey , and a certificate initializer. If those containers can’t communicate with each other, nothing works.

Thankfully, I’m a weird nerd who also runs a CasaOS deployment on another machine. After I executed the bin/setup script there, everything worked as it should. The next issue was flashing back to the latest TRMNL firmware package. My unit arrived with FW 1.5.12, well behind the current 1.8.18 release.

Flashing proved to be an annoyance again because I struggled to keep the unit in flashing mode and get the web flasher to communicate with the serial port on my Fedora PC. After about 30 minutes of troubleshooting without making progress, I switched to my MacBook Pro, where the process worked on the first try. Go figure.

Once you’ve updated the display to the proper firmware and pointed its connections at your server, you can write and design your own display templates. If starting from scratch isn’t your thing, TRMNL’s own plugins repo and a community-maintained catalog are available. A new Extensions Gallery in the Terminus web UI lets you import certain plugins for local hosting.

The options are almost overwhelming, and I imagine it will take some time to get everything dialed in exactly as I want it. I still plan to stick with the BYOS route, but the process isn’t as straightforward as I had hoped. For example, the setting for pointing the display at your local server is hidden under the “advanced” settings page during the web portal login.

Real-world impressions

Once I deployed the display in my kitchen, I could get a better sense of how it would fit into my day-to-day life. The 7.5-inch e-paper display is large enough to read from across the room, and all the plugins I had running looked crisp and legible. My son was enamored with the lunar cycles display and commented that “now I’ll always know what moon we have.”

That’s where the kit shines: showing little rotating bursts of useful information that you might never have thought to look up before.

Seeed Studio says the display can run for three months on battery power. I haven’t had the device long enough to verify that claim, but I’m not sure I need the battery for much more than backup. The device powers via USB just fine, so I’ll probably leave it connected to a nearby hub on the counter. The three-month estimate assumes that the display will update once every six hours. I prefer refreshes closer to once an hour, which would cut battery life significantly. Either way, the battery becomes largely irrelevant if you use a USB power source.

Final thoughts

The official TRMNL route is starting to look mighty tempting if it means getting the type of headache-free, set-it-and-forget-it Ron Popeil experience I was expecting from this setup. I’ll keep tinkering with the BYOS solutions, but since those still run on the official TRMNL firmware, I may switch back and use the rest of my 14-day trial to see what best suits my needs. The $50 license fee would push my total project cost over $100. That’s not a huge deal, but it’s double what I was expecting.

The TRMNL/Seeed Studio collaboration has produced a true DIY device. It will never compete with a home assistant device from Amazon or Apple, but it’s not meant to, and that’s a good thing. Not everyone wants a digital butler waiting for their next command. Sometimes you just want information that’s relevant to you and your life, displayed in a central place in your home.

I got a B&W version a year ago and got a color this year. Both work great. I use Home Assistant and ESPHome to flash the device and then use Home Assistant dashboards and Puppet to display on the devices. I found it much easier to develop my dashboards in Home Assistant than manually. Never tried TRML because I didn't want another subscription. SenseCraft wasn't out back then, so I never tried it. Here's my write up for the B&W version: https://forum.seeedstudio.com/t/xiao-7-5-epaper-panel-home-assistant-dashboard/293307 And for the color version: https://forum.seeedstudio.com/t/ret...paper-display-home-assistant-dashboard/294823 View attachment 146638

stories.title: No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham

stories.body:
Andy Burnham and his wife took the plane to the United Nations in the US in September

Published 1 hour ago

Downing Street has defended sending the official UK government plane to Manchester to pick up Andy Burnham, rather than the prime minister travelling to London in advance of the flight.

The Airbus A321neo departed London Stansted Airport for Saint John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at about 06:00 on Monday without the prime minister on board.

Half an hour later it landed in Manchester to collect Burnham, before taking off again to cross the Atlantic for the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm).

The trip sparked a backlash on social media with some questioning the value for money, but Number 10 said security, cost and "operational requirements" were all factored in.

The official UK government plane , carrying the registration G-GBNI, is often used by British prime ministers and royals for overseas trips.

Flight tracking data shows the jet made a 35 minute flight on Monday morning to Manchester, where it spent an hour and a half on the tarmac, before taking off at 08:00 to head to St John's.

In response, Tory MP and shadow cabinet minister Neil O'Brien accused Labour of managing to "waste taxpayers' money and jet fuel so they can posture".

"You have to pay through the nose for energy and fuel to pursue their Net Zero obsession... But when it's them, the rules are different," he added.

Asked why Burnham had not travelled to London instead, his official spokesperson told reporters: "The prime minister's travel arrangements reflect where he was carrying out official government business at the end of last week.

"As you know, he spent the day in Scotland on Friday; returned to Manchester to work from Number 10 North on Friday evening."

The official UK Government plane is used for the PM and royals

Burnham will meet Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday, coming at the end of the King's Caribbean tour , with the prime minister saying he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery.

It is unclear how much the London to Manchester trip cost, or whether there is a precedent for it, as the Cabinet Office's transparency data for the plane only lists overseas trips.

None of Burnham's trips are listed yet, as the data is published quarterly.

The latest data for April to June 2026 shows then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer made four round trips on the jet, including a £121,000 trip to Armenia with 21 officials for the European Political Community Summit.

A trip from the UK to Paris in April cost £39,000.

The precise cost of each flight can depend on how many officials were with the prime minister, fuel costs and other factors such as landing fees.

It is also unclear whether transporting the prime minister, his security detail and officials by train or road transport from Manchester to Stansted would have been much cheaper.

A previous version of the UK government official plane, an RAF Voyager, was given a £900,000 repaint job in 2020 before being replaced with a different plane.

A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities

Donald Trump ’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.

The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.

The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.

But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.

The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.

The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.

Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.

By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.

China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.

It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions . While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.

Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.

China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions , covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.

One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.

China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.

This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?

The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

stories.title: Rewriting Copyright Law for Generative AI Would Hurt Everyone
stories.summary: In courts across the country, publishers and creators are suing large AI companies for training generative AI models on copyrighted works. It’s easy to see these cases as a David-and-Goliath showdown between authors and publishers fighting for a cut of Big Tech company profits. But this fight is actually much larger. It affects billions of people who aren’t represented in the case at all, including researchers, artists, activists, journalists, people with disabilities, and anyone who accesses and shares content online. That’s why EFF is stepping in to defend the public’s rights in these cases. Today, EFF filed an amicus brief in In re OpenAI, explaining how the court’s ruling on fair use could impact people worldwide. If fair use gets narrowed, it will impede work that benefits the public, like medical research and investigative journalism, and even limit access to privacy protection tools. Let’s be clear: creators and workers deserve support as AI changes their fields, and Big Tech companies must be held accountable for the harms they cause. But giving copyright holders more control over the web won’t accomplish either of these goals. If the plaintiffs prevail in these cases, courts would have to rewrite copyright law in ways that hurt everyone except powerful media and tech companies. Rewriting Fair Use Makes Everyone Worse Off Copyright exists for one reason: to stimulate creativity and innovation in service of the greater public good. Unfortunately, the plaintiffs in this lawsuit are arguing to limit everyone’s fair use rights, in ways that would thwart the basic purpose of copyright. The harms of shrinking fair use will go far beyond generative AI, impacting everyone. Initial speculation that AI models would be infringement machines, churning out works highly similar to those on which they were trained, has proven unfounded . And courts have already found fair use in cases where copyrighted works were used to train generative AI models, recognizing that training uses those works for a fundamentally different purpose . Plaintiffs in these cases argue that, even if the use is transformative, using their works to train AI is still unfair, because the AI models could generate new, non-infringing works that might compete with plaintiffs’ own works. Cost of living has loomed over this election cycle as workers and unions champion candidates fighting for higher wages and tackling rising prices

For millions of Americans heading to the polls on Tuesday, affordability is a constant and worsening issue, and it’s been a prevailing concern this election cycle.

In Lorain county, Ohio , Gina Jones and her co-workers at the Lorain county job and family services have been on strike since February 2026, the longest public sector strike in Ohio history and on pace to break the US record for longest public sector strike.

Ohio voted for Donald Trump in 2024 by more than 5%. As the final day of voting nears, Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has a slight lead on Republican Senate incumbent Jon Husted in polling, and the economy has been a key factor in the fight.

“They don’t pay a living wage any more. They used to,” Jones said. “Our healthcare coverage has stayed the same, but the cost of it has changed significantly. It used to be $35 a month for a family. In January it’s going to be $600 a month for a family for the same coverage.”

She said as wages have lagged, with starting pay at about $15 an hour , health insurance costs have eaten up any wage gains to the extent that some employees are making less than when they started.

Negotiations for a new union contract broke down with the county, now led by three Republican commissioners, as workers are pushing for a $1 an hour increase to their base pay.

Daniel Petticord, the deputy director of the Lorain county jobs and family services, said in an email “management believes it recognizes the important efforts of our bargaining unit employees while maintaining fiscal responsibility,” and blamed the union for walking away from negotiations.

“We service the clients of Lorain county that are the poorest of the community, and some of the people that work at jobs and family services qualify for those same services,” Jones said. “We’re hoping that with the Ohio governor election, that we get somebody in there who will be in favor of labor and see the fact that people don’t make a living wage in Lorain county any more.”

In Minnesota, Bob Mattila, a special education paraprofessional in Minneapolis and SEIU Local 284 member, is looking for elected officials who will back state legislation that would increase pay for himself and his co-workers to $25 an hour and to lower their costs for health insurance.

“We simply aren’t paid enough to do the vitally important work that we do,” Mattila said. “I even take state health insurance because they decided I don’t make enough money.

“Money, power and respect. Those three things are critical to what we need out of our work and what we deserve from our elected officials,” he added. “Having very labor-friendly people in places of power is going to give workers like me things that we need to live, because we’re at a point where I can’t afford to put $50 of gas every time when I fill up my car when I’m not even making $25 an hour.”

Labor leaders see a real advantage for Democrats now that so much focus is on the economy.

“The labor movement’s been talking about the issues that affect workers and the kitchen table for decades, and we’re now seeing that everybody else got the memo,” said Liz Shuler, president of the AFL-CIO, the largest federation of labor unions in the US, which has been pushing to turn out 16 million union family voters this election.

“It’s pervasive. Everywhere I travel, every campaign that you see is talking about what working people are struggling through, and it’s the cost of gas, groceries, rent and healthcare, but it’s also the fact that our pay just can’t keep up with the rising prices.”

In Detroit, Michigan, another key battleground state, 27-year-old Bailee Porter, who has worked at Detroit Diesel and is a member of the United Auto Workers, has been canvassing for candidates such as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the US Senate, citing his support for Medicare for All, which the UAW has also backed .

She said rising prices of basic necessities have made budgeting and cutting back on essentials like groceries a common worry.

“It’s just costly on every aspect. It’s disrupting people’s routines, so it’s ridiculous. Food, gas. I don’t even want to talk about utility bills. It’s just insane,” said Porter. “Things should be affordable. Your basic necessities have to be affordable. There’s just no other way around it. They have to be. Legislation needs to be changed or enforced or written to where it can help the middle class and labor.”

But the financial struggles experienced by many Americans are unlikely to be easily alleviated no matter who wins the midterms. Joe Biden, the US’s most pro-labor president in recent history, also failed to appease voters who were feeling left behind.

Researchers have noted the federal government’s definition of and tracking of poverty doesn’t account for the struggles Americans are facing, as the federal poverty line is outdated from the 1960s and doesn’t account for geographic discrepancies in costs of living.

“The percent of people that are struggling is so much higher than our official statistics are revealing,” said Dr Stephanie Hoopes, an economist and director of United for Alice. “These are often people who are keeping our economy running smoothly and fueling our economic growth, and yet they’re struggling to support their own families.”

41.3% of US households, more than 54.5m households, faced financial hardship in 2024, according to a 2026 report by United for Alice.

12.5% of US households made under the federal poverty level threshold, an income of $15,060 annually for a single individual and $31,200 for a family of four.

28.8% of US households were Alice: asset limited, income constrained and employed. These households earn above the federal poverty level but did not make enough money to afford basic expenses in the county where they live.

2025 and 2026 projected data shows the costs of basic necessities continuing to outpace overall inflation.

“By some measures, our economy is doing great, unemployment rate is low, stock markets booming, productivity and GDP are growing,” Hoopes added. “But when you look at things like how many households are Alice [asset limited, income constrained and employed], and that number continuing to increase, and wages lagging behind the cost of living, there’s some real concerns in the economy.”

For Shunda Whitfield, a certified nursing assistant in St Louis, Missouri, those economic concerns can be life-threatening.

She has been struggling with a recent spike in costs for her medication for lupus, an autoimmune disease.

“I sometimes have to choose between if I’m going to get my medication or if I’m going to get groceries in house due to the fact that my medicine is going up,” said Whitfield, who has been struggling to afford a recent spike in costs for her lupus medication.

“You have to juggle things around to make sure you have cash to get to work to make the money to afford groceries or your medication,” she added. “I would like to see people get out here and vote to put people in place that are for the working people and not just for the billionaires.”

stories.title: Poundland's former owner offers to invest as minister prepares to meet board
stories.summary: Wolverhampton's Steve Smith said he wants to put some money back into the firm he started.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Poundland has been given until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk.

Published 4 hours ago

Poundland's founder has said he would invest in the firm and a government minister said she would meet the firm's board amid its administration fears.

Steve Smith, who set-up the Walsall-based business, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year.

The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency.

US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it.

Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for £1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).

The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk.

Steven Smith founded Poundland in 1990 with the help of his father, Kevin Smith

It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk.

The meeting was first reported by Sky News.

There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers.

Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of £30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for £1.

More on Poundland

'Poundland closure would leave a void in our town' Published 2 days ago

Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators Published 4 days ago

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected.

Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table.

"And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there."

He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year.

"Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy."

Staff held a protest outside Poundland's Walsall-based HQ last week

He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse.

"This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added.

The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well".

Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now".

"Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street."

'Get on the case now'

"Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added.

In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".

"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."

Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids."

The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders."

stories.body:
The cyberattack on crypto-asset exchange Binance is potentially the largest theft of its kind on record. Binance has estimated the assets stolen at an eye-watering US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion).

On October 29, 2026, analytics firms reported that large amounts of crypto-assets had been moved from wallets used by the exchange across multiple blockchain networks – a digital system for recording transactions that is run collectively by its users. Most of the money was moved within a period of about 20 minutes.

In response, Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals telling users that it would cover losses using its emergency protection fund and corporate resources. Around US$3 billion of the affected assets was frozen by October 30, according to Binance. However, freezing funds is not the same as recovering them.

As of November 1, Binance says it has restored 95% of the stolen assets. But much of this has come from various funds held by the exchange, as well as its corporate treasury. It has now started to re-open withdrawals in phases . The exchange has promised to publish a full incident report once the investigation is completed.

Investigators say that indicators point to North Korea-linked cybercriminals . But attribution should remain provisional until the evidence is fully established. So how might the attackers have breached Binance?

The emerging explanation points primarily to a compromise of the systems that authorise withdrawals in Binance, rather than a successful attack on the underlying blockchains used for individual crypto-assets such as Bitcoin or Ether.

Binance initially suggested that an engineer’s laptop had been compromised, potentially enabling attackers to access internal services and initiate unauthorised transactions. However, subsequent statements indicated that additional parts of the system had been breached. So it would be premature to treat the laptop as the complete explanation.

A useful analogy is a bank vault. An attacker may not need to break the vault itself if they can manipulate the system that tells it when to release funds. In crypto-asset exchanges, so-called signing infrastructure performs this authorisation function.

Investigators believe that attackers were able to obtain or misuse valid authorisations , allowing assets to be transferred out of wallets controlled by the exchange. Binance says that it has found no evidence that private keys for wallets – used to authorise outgoing blockchain transactions – were leaked.

One reported element in this was Ethereum’s EIP-7702 feature, which gives conventional crypto-asset wallets functions that they wouldn’t normally have. Investigators observed that authorisations linked to this feature had apparently enabled attacker-controlled code to move assets.

These assets included funds arriving after the initial compromise. However, it does not, by itself, establish a flaw in Ethereum’s underlying consensus mechanism. The consensus mechanism is the set of rules for transactions agreed upon by the decentralised network.

How secure is cryptocurrency?

A central lesson is that the security of a blockchain must be distinguished from the security of the wider ecosystem built around it. A blockchain may maintain a highly resilient and tamper-resistant transaction record. On the other hand, an exchange, wallet provider or other intermediary may be vulnerable.

Compromised staff credentials, defective access controls, malicious code or weaknesses in transaction approval processes can all act as entry points for cybercriminals.

This also highlights that many crypto-asset services are not decentralised. Many exchanges are highly centralised in their custody arrangements, governance and control over customers’ assets. Such concentration can create single points of failure. The decentralised nature of a blockchain does not remove the need for effective governance of the businesses operating on it.

The speed and cross-border nature of the theft further complicate enforcement. Stolen assets can be moved through different blockchain networks, swapped into other tokens or channelled through decentralised finance protocols.

Some issuers of a type of crypto-asset called stablecoins (these act a bit like fiat currencies such as the US dollar) can freeze tokens under their control. This has helped limit losses from the Binance theft. Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ether generally cannot be frozen in the same way by an issuer. These differences matter enormously for tracing, recovery and investor protection.

There is also a growing concern about AI-enabled cybercrime. AI agents may increase the speed, scale and sophistication of attacks on automated financial systems. However, there is currently no established evidence that AI agents carried out this particular hack; the broader risk should not be confused with a confirmed cause.

Investors and financial stability

For investors, this incident is a reminder that owning a crypto-asset involves more than exposure to its market price. There are also custody, cybersecurity, operational, “counterparty” risks (the exposure organisations have to another body or individual that may default on their obligations) and legal risks.

Investors should understand who holds their assets, whether customer funds are segregated (that crypto-assets are not used by an exchange or broker to fund their daily operations), what security and recovery arrangements exist and what legal protections apply if an exchange fails.

They should not assume that crypto holdings enjoy the deposit insurance or central bank safety nets available with some traditional banking activities.

The wider financial stability implications depend on the extent of the connections between conventional banking and cryptocurrencies. Traditional financial institutions are increasingly exploring distributed ledger technology (a digital system that stores and shares data across a decentralised network of computers) – seen in blockchain networks – for tokenisation (a data security feature), payments and settlement. Some banks also facilitate investment exposure to Bitcoin, Ether and other digital assets.

Nevertheless, as financial institutions, funds and payment systems become more connected to crypto markets, operational shocks and losses could transmit more widely through the system.

Practical responses

My research on crypto-assets, decentralised finance and financial regulation consistently emphasises that innovation must be accompanied by accountability, effective governance and proportionate safeguards.

Four priorities stand out. First, exchanges need rigorous cybersecurity and operational resilience standards. This includes independent security testing, tightly controlled access privileges, secure signing systems, transaction limits, continuous monitoring and credible plans for responding to incidents like the Binance theft.

Second, regulators should assess actual control and governance arrangements rather than accepting labels such as “decentralised” at face value. Entities exercising custody or operational control should have clear obligations.

Third, consumer protection must be strengthened through the segregation of customer assets, transparent custody practices, clear risk disclosures and workable insolvency and recovery arrangements. Any compensation arrangements should be clearly explained rather than assumed.

Fourth, international cooperation is indispensable . Regulators, law enforcement, exchanges, stablecoin issuers and blockchain analytics providers must be able to coordinate rapidly to trace illicit transfers, preserve evidence and freeze assets where legally possible.

This case brings a broader message to the surface, which is that technological sophistication is not a substitute for sound governance. Confidence in digital finance will ultimately depend on the resilience of its infrastructure, the accountability of those who control it and the effectiveness of the regulatory framework protecting users and the wider financial system.
